blocks.title: Simple Counting Problems
teacherCues: Pose: Draw two numbers from 1–8 with replacement to sum 12. Ask pairs to list all ways.
After Example 2: What changed when we did not replace? Why did the count drop?

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine drawing numbered tickets from a hat for a raffle. If you put the ticket back, you could draw the same number again. Counting how many ways a certain sum can happen is a real‑world puzzle that starts with careful listing.

explanation: A [[kw:simple counting problem]] asks you to list all possible outcomes of a small experiment.
When an item is put back before the next draw, the selection is [[kw:with replacement]].
When the item is not returned, the selection is [[kw:without replacement]].
If you list every possibility, you can just count them to find the answer.

visuals.title: Ways to sum to 12 from numbers 1–8

formulaCard.title: Counting by Listing
notes: Best when the total number of outcomes is small.
With replacement may produce duplicate pairs; without replacement forbids equal numbers.

examples.title: A – With Replacement
examples.prompt: How many ways can you draw two numbers from 1 to 8, with replacement, to obtain a sum of 12?
steps: List all pairs whose sum is $ 12 $: start with first number $ 4 $, then second $ 8 $, etc.
Check both orders: $ (4,8) $ works, and $ (8,4) $ works.
The pair $ (6,6) $ is possible because we replace the paper.

examples.title: B – Without Replacement
examples.prompt: How many ways can you draw two different numbers from 1 to 8 to get a sum of 12?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why is the pair (6,6) not allowed this time? How does that change the total?
steps: List pairs with first number $ 4 $: $ (4,8) $, $ (8,4) $; first number $ 5 $: $ (5,7) $, $ (7,5) $.
Because we do not replace, the two numbers must be different, so $ (6,6) $ is impossible.
Count only the $ 4 $ distinct ordered pairs.

examples.title: C – Quick Check
examples.prompt: If you want a sum of 14 with the same setup, how many ways exist with replacement? (Numbers from 1 to 8.)

confusionCorner.title: With vs. Without Replacement
confusionCorner.body: In [[imp:without replacement]], you cannot pick the same number twice. The pair (6,6) is only possible [[imp:with replacement]]. Always check the selection method before counting!

questions.prompt: When the drawn item is put back before the next draw, the selection is called ___.
hints: The key phrase describes returning the item.

questions.prompt: In Example 1 (with replacement), how many ways are there to get a sum of 12?
hints: Check the table of ordered pairs.

questions.prompt: Does 'without replacement' allow the pair (7,7)? Answer yes or no.
hints: Without replacement means the numbers must be different.
Think: can you draw the same paper twice?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: No, without replacement you cannot draw the same number twice.

blocks.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle
teacherCues: Explain: If you have 3 shirts and 4 pants, how many outfits? Multiply 3 × 4 = 12.
Show the extended principle with three events (lock combination).

discoveryHook.scenario: You're customizing a new car: 5 colors, 3 engine choices, and 2 interior styles. Instead of listing every combination, the Fundamental Counting Principle lets you multiply and instantly know: $5 \times 3 \times 2 = 30$ possibilities!

explanation: If an event $ E_1 $ can happen in $ m_1 $ ways, and after that $ E_2 $ can happen in $ m_2 $ ways, then the two events together can happen in $ m_1 \times m_2 $ ways.
For three or more events, multiply the number of ways for each: $ m_1 \times m_2 \times m_3 $.
It saves you from listing all possibilities when the count is large.

rows.1: 8 choices for 1st digit, 10 each for other 6

formulaCard.title: Fundamental Counting Principle
notes: $ m_i $ is the number of ways the $ i $th event can occur after previous events.
Applies when events occur one after another.

examples.title: A – Two-letter Pairs
examples.prompt: How many different pairs of letters from the English alphabet can be formed?
steps: First event: choose first letter – $ 26 $ ways.
Second event: choose second letter – $ 26 $ ways.

examples.title: B – Catalog Number
examples.prompt: A catalog number has one letter followed by a five-digit number (00000–99999). How many different numbers are possible?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why do we multiply, not add, the number of letter choices and digit choices?
steps: Five-digit number: each digit $ 10 $ choices, so $ 10^5 = 100000 $ ways.

examples.title: C – Simple Outfits
examples.prompt: You have 4 shirts and 5 pairs of pants. How many different outfits can you make?

confusionCorner.title: Multiply When Sequential
confusionCorner.body: The principle uses multiplication because each choice of the first event can be paired with every choice of the second. Adding $ m_1 + m_2 $ would count separate, unpaired options.

questions.prompt: The rule that says if event $ A $ has $ m $ ways and event $ B $ has $ n $ ways, then both events together can occur in $ m \times n $ ways is called the ___.
In a phone number within an area code, how many choices are there for the first digit? (Hint: cannot be 0 or 1.)
If a menu offers 3 appetizers and 7 main courses, how many ordered pairs of one appetizer and one main course are possible?

blocks.title: Permutations of n Elements
teacherCues: Write A, B, C on the board and ask students to list all orders. Then generalize to n elements.
Emphasize the factorial notation and connect to the idea of arranging all distinct objects.

discoveryHook.scenario: A musician has 6 different songs to play in a set. Deciding the order can change the whole vibe of the performance. Counting all possible setlists is really a permutation problem!

explanation: A [[kw:permutation]] is an ordering of a set of distinct elements.
The number of ways to arrange all $ n $ elements is $ n! $ (n factorial).
For 6 letters A–F, there are $ 6! = 720 $ different orders.

formulaCard.title: Permutations of n Elements
notes: Used when order matters and all elements are distinct.

examples.title: A – Arrange 6 Letters
examples.prompt: How many different ways can the letters A, B, C, D, E, F be arranged?
steps: First position: any of the $ 6 $ letters.
Second position: any of the remaining $ 5 $ letters.

examples.title: B – Arranging 4 Letters
examples.prompt: How many permutations of the letters W, X, Y, Z are possible?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why is factorial the shortcut for counting all orders without having to draw a tree?

examples.title: C – Book Arrangement
examples.prompt: You have 5 different books to place on a shelf. How many different orders are possible?

confusionCorner.title: Zero Factorial
confusionCorner.body: Don't be surprised: $ 0! = 1 $ by definition. This makes formulas for permutations and combinations work smoothly even when $ n = r $.

questions.prompt: An ordering of a set of distinct elements is called a ___.
If you have 3 colored balls (red, blue, green), how many distinct sequences can you form by arranging all three?

blocks.title: Permutations of n Taken r and Distinguishable Permutations
teacherCues: Show the horse race example: 8 horses, pick 1st, 2nd, 3rd. Lead to nPr formula.
Write BANANA and ask: How many orders? Then introduce distinguishable permutations formula.

discoveryHook.scenario: In a race with 8 horses, only the top 3 places matter for medals. You're not arranging all 8—just picking and ordering 3. And when some horses are identical twins (letters repeating), some arrangements look the same, so you need a clever correction.

explanation: Choosing an ordered subset of $ r $ from $ n $ distinct elements gives a [[kw:permutation of n taken r at a time]]: $ {}_nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} $.

When some elements are identical, the total $ n! $ overcounts arrangements that look the same. Use [[kw:distinguishable permutations]]: $ \frac{n!}{n_1! n_2! \cdots n_k!} $ where $ n_i $ are counts of identical items.

rows.0: List r ordered from n distinct

formulaCard.title: Two Permutation Formulas
notes: In nPr, order matters and no repetition of elements.
Distinguishable: use when items repeat; calculate as if all distinct then divide by factorials of duplicates.

examples.title: A – Horse Race (nPr)
examples.prompt: Eight horses run; how many ways can they finish 1st, 2nd, and 3rd?

examples.title: B – BANANA letters
examples.prompt: How many distinguishable arrangements of the word BANANA are possible?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why do we divide by 3! and 2!? What would happen if we didn't?
steps: Divide by $ 3! $ for the 3 identical A's and $ 2! $ for the 2 identical N's: $ \frac{720}{6 \cdot 2} = 60 $.

examples.title: C – Club Officers
examples.prompt: A club has 5 members. How many ways to choose a president and vice-president (order matters)?

confusionCorner.title: Order Matters!
confusionCorner.body: Permutations always consider order. Choosing a president and vice‑president is a permutation (President A, VP B is different from President B, VP A). We'll soon contrast this with combinations where order doesn't matter.

hints: Start from 8 and multiply downward 3 terms.

questions.prompt: The word MISSISSIPPI has 1 M, 4 I's, 4 S's, and 2 P's. The number of distinguishable arrangements is $ \frac{11!}{4!4!2!1} $, which equals ___.
hints: The formula divides by factorials of repeated counts.

questions.prompt: How many permutations of 2 letters taken from the set {A, B, C} are possible? (Order matters.)

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid — Combinations (Order Doesn't Matter)
teacherCues: Contrast with permutations: a committee of 3 people (order irrelevant) vs. a 1st, 2nd, 3rd place.
Show the nCr formula and explain the extra r! in the denominator to remove order.

discoveryHook.scenario: You're choosing 3 desserts from a menu of 10 to bring to a party. You don't care who brings what—just which three you have. That's a combination, and it cuts the number of possibilities dramatically.

explanation: A [[kw:combination]] is a selection of $ r $ items from $ n $ distinct items where order does not matter.
Understand: first count permutations ($ nPr $), then divide by $ r! $ because each unordered group appears in $ r! $ different orders.
Combinations are used when only the group matters, not the arrangement.

formulaCard.title: Combination (nCr)
notes: Key check: order not important → combination.

examples.title: A – Choosing a Committee
examples.prompt: How many ways can a 3‑person committee be selected from 8 people?
steps: We only care who is on the committee, not the order they are chosen.

examples.title: B – Pizza Toppings
examples.prompt: A pizza place offers 12 toppings. You want 4 different toppings. How many possible pizzas?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: If you instead cared about the order the toppings are placed, would it still be a combination? Why?
steps: Order of toppings doesn't matter for the final pizza.

examples.title: C – Handshakes
examples.prompt: There are 6 people at a meeting. If everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once, how many handshakes occur?
steps: A handshake involves 2 people, order irrelevant.

confusionCorner.title: The Extra r!
confusionCorner.body: To go from permutation ($ {}_8P_3 = 336 $) to combination ($ {}_8C_3 = 56 $) you divide by $ 3! = 6 $ because each group of 3 people can be arranged in 6 ways. This removes the ordering that permutations count.

questions.prompt: A selection of items where order does not matter is called a ___.
hints: The formula has an extra r! in the denominator compared to permutation.

questions.prompt: From a group of 5 friends, you want to invite 2 to a movie. How many different pairs can you invite?

challengeCorner.prompt: A bag contains 3 red, 4 blue, and 2 green marbles. How many ways can you choose 2 marbles of the same color?
hints: Break into cases: both red, both blue, both green.
challengeCorner.feedbackIfWrong: Compute each case: red ${}_3C_2 = 3$, blue ${}_4C_2 = 6$, green ${}_2C_2 = 1$. Sum = 10.
